assessment.summary: KRAS is one of the most extensively studied oncology targets, with 556 high-resolution PDB structures (best 0.953Å), over 5,900 ChEMBL IC50 entries, and two FDA-approved covalent inhibitors (sotorasib and adagrasib) targeting the G12C mutation. Druggability is high for the G12C mutant allele specifically, though targeting other KRAS mutations (G12D, G12V, G13D, etc.) remains an active and partially unresolved challenge. The overall evidence base is exceptionally strong across structural, chemical, and literature dimensions.
evidence_gaps: Approved drugs (sotorasib, adagrasib) are covalent and mutation-specific (G12C only); druggability of other common KRAS mutations (G12D, G12V, G12R, G13D, Q61H) is less established with no approved drugs yet
Median IC50 of ~1020 nM across ChEMBL entries suggests many compounds have modest potency, and the chemical space for non-covalent pan-KRAS inhibitors is still maturing
Resistance mechanisms to G12C inhibitors (e.g., secondary KRAS mutations, bypass signalling via RTKs, MAPK reactivation) are not fully solved and limit clinical durability
Wild-type KRAS selectivity window: therapeutic index for tumour vs. normal tissue is not fully characterised for newer non-covalent approaches
Combination strategies needed for most KRAS-driven cancers (e.g., pancreatic) are still under investigation and optimal partners are unknown
Allosteric vs. active-site inhibitor profiles for non-G12C mutants lack clinical validation
